title: Capacitors — Charge Storage (tau = R*C) and Power-Rail Decoupling

blocks.x: Goal

Calculate how fast a **capacitor** charges or discharges through a resistor using the **RC time constant** ($\tau = R \cdot C$) in Falstad, and place a $100\text{ nF}$ ($0.1\ \mu\text{F}$) **decoupling capacitor** across a microcontroller's power pins to prevent motor current spikes from resetting the chip.

items.x: **New ideas (max 2):**

**Capacitor charge storage and RC time constant ($\tau = R \cdot C$)**: How two conductive plates separated by an insulator store charge in Farads (`F`, `µF`, `nF`) and resist sudden changes in **voltage** with characteristic time $\tau = R \cdot C$ ($63.2\%$ in $1\tau$, $\approx 99.3\%$ in $5\tau$).

**Power-rail decoupling (bypass) capacitors**: Combining a fast $0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ ceramic capacitor and a larger $100\ \mu\text{F}$ bulk electrolytic capacitor in parallel across `VCC` and `GND` as a local charge reservoir.
**New syntax:** Python `math.exp` for the charge curve and `ValueError` guards; Falstad Capacitor (`c`) and Oscilloscope (`o`) elements in circuit netlists.
**Target time (unmeasured — [log yours](../.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/beginner-timing-log.md)):** Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.0 hours

blocks.x: Idea 1: Capacitor charge storage and RC time constant ($\tau = R \cdot C$)

items.x: **Primary resource:** [SparkFun — Capacitors](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/capacitors) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`
**What to read:** Read exact headings **`Introduction`**, **`Symbols and Units`**, **`Capacitor Theory`**, **`Charging and Discharging`**, and **`Capacitor Types`**.
**What to skip:** Skip **`Capacitors in Series/Parallel`** and **`Application Examples -> Signal Filtering`**.

**Key takeaway:** A **capacitor** acts like a tiny, ultra-fast rechargeable bucket that stores electrical charge on two conductive plates separated by an insulator, measured in **Farads (`F`)**—typically **microfarads (`µF`, $10^{-6}\text{ F}$)** or **nanofarads (`nF`, $10^{-9}\text{ F}$)**. Because moving charge onto the plates takes time, **a capacitor's voltage cannot change instantly**. When charged through a resistor $R$, the **RC time constant** $\tau = R \cdot C$ (in seconds) tells you the exact time needed to cover $63.2\%$ of the remaining voltage step (reaching $\approx 99.3\%$ after $5\tau$).

**Alternative resource:** [PhET — Capacitor Lab: Basics](https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/capacitor-lab-basics) `[verify in-app]` — Connect the battery to the parallel plates `[verify in-app]` to watch charge accumulate until $V_C = V_{\text{battery}}$.

blocks.x: Idea 2: Power-rail decoupling (bypass) capacitors

items.x: **Primary resource:** [SparkFun — Capacitors ("Decoupling (Bypass) Capacitors" & "Power Supply Filtering")](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/capacitors) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`
**What to read:** Read exact headings **`Application Examples`**, **`Decoupling (Bypass) Capacitors`**, and **`Power Supply Filtering`**.
**What to skip:** Skip audio crossover sections.

**Key takeaway:** When a heavy load or digital chip suddenly demands a burst of current, the parasitic resistance of long battery wires causes the $5.0\text{ V}$ supply rail to dip ("brown out"), which can reboot a microcontroller mid-motion. Placing a **$0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ ($100\text{ nF}$) ceramic decoupling capacitor** right next to the chip's `VCC` and `GND` pins (paired with a **$100\ \mu\text{F}$ electrolytic bulk capacitor** where power enters the breadboard) supplies that instant current burst locally and keeps the voltage rail rock-steady.

blocks.x: Bridge Notes

When a capacitor $C$ (starting at $0\text{ V}$) charges toward $V_{\text{supply}}$ through a series resistor $R$, its voltage $V_C(t)$ at time $t$ follows an exponential curve governed by the **RC time constant** $\tau = R \cdot C$:
Check the units carefully: multiplying Ohms ($\Omega$) by Farads ($\text{F}$) produces **seconds ($\text{s}$)**:

items.x: If $R = 10\text{ k}\Omega = 10{,}000\ \Omega$ and $C = 100\ \mu\text{F} = 0.000100\text{ F}$, then $\tau = 10{,}000 \times 0.000100 = 1.0\text{ s}$.
At $t = 1\tau$ ($1.0\text{ s}$), the capacitor reaches $1 - e^{-1} \approx 63.2\%$ of $V_{\text{supply}}$ ($3.16\text{ V}$ on a $5.0\text{ V}$ supply).
At $t = 2\tau$ ($2.0\text{ s}$), the capacitor reaches $1 - e^{-2} \approx 86.5\%$ of $V_{\text{supply}}$ ($4.32\text{ V}$).
At $t = 5\tau$ ($5.0\text{ s}$), the capacitor reaches $1 - e^{-5} \approx 99.3\%$ of $V_{\text{supply}}$ ($4.97\text{ V}$—effectively fully charged).

blocks.x: *(Safety note on polarized capacitors: Small ceramic decoupling capacitors like $0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ / $100\text{ nF}$ are **unpolarized** and can be inserted either way. Larger cylindrical aluminum **electrolytic** capacitors like $100\ \mu\text{F}$ are **polarized**: the shorter leg marked with a **`-` stripe** MUST connect to `GND`!)*

Common mistakes & troubleshooting

items.x: **Wiring a polarized electrolytic capacitor backward (`-` stripe to `5V` instead of `GND`):** Reverse voltage breaks down the thin oxide layer inside an electrolytic capacitor, causing it to overheat and pop! Always connect the shorter lead with the **`-` stripe** to `GND`.

**Placing the $0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ decoupling capacitor far away from the chip on the breadboard:** Long jumper wires add parasitic impedance that blocks fast current pulses; always place the $0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ ceramic capacitor as close as physically possible to the IC's `VCC` and `GND` pins.

blocks.x: Check yourself

items.x: **Unit conversion (`nF` to `µF`):** Ceramic decoupling capacitors are often labeled **`100 nF`** (100 nanofarads). Since $1\ \mu\text{F} = 1{,}000\text{ nF}$, how many microfarads (`µF`) is $100\text{ nF}$?

blocks.x: $\frac{100\text{ nF}}{1000} = \mathbf{0.1\ \mu\text{F}}$. (`100 nF` and `0.1 µF` are two names for the exact same capacitor!)

items.x: **Calculating $1\tau$ and $5\tau$:** A sensor filter uses a $1\text{ k}\Omega$ ($1{,}000\ \Omega$) resistor and a $10\ \mu\text{F}$ ($0.000010\text{ F}$) capacitor. What is the RC time constant $\tau = R \cdot C$ in milliseconds (`ms`), and how long does it take to reach $\approx 99.3\%$ ($5\tau$)?

blocks.x: $\tau = 1{,}000\ \Omega \times 0.000010\text{ F} = 0.010\text{ s} = \mathbf{10\text{ ms}}$, so $5\tau = \mathbf{50\text{ ms}}$.

items.x: **Why decoupling matters in robotics:** Your microcontroller runs fine when blinking an LED, but reboots every time a heavy load on the same power supply switches on. Which components across the power rails fix this brownout?

blocks.x: A **$100\ \mu\text{F}$ bulk electrolytic capacitor** across the breadboard power rails (to buffer surge current) plus a **$0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ ($100\text{ nF}$) ceramic decoupling capacitor** across the microcontroller's `VCC` and `GND` pins.
Recap

items.x: A **capacitor** ($C$, in Farads `F`) stores charge and resists sudden changes in **voltage** ($V$), charging $63.2\%$ in one **RC time constant** $\tau = R \cdot C$ and $\approx 99.3\%$ in $5\tau$.
**Decoupling capacitors** ($0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ ceramic near logic chips + $100\ \mu\text{F}$ electrolytic on power rails) act as local charge reservoirs that prevent supply voltage dips.
